2.tip: ESD hurts what's INSIDE the case: RAM, CPU, motherboard. Plugging in speakers or a display from outside is safe.
2.why: Electrostatic discharge can fry the tiny circuits on bare chips. When you install RAM you touch exposed memory chips and contacts, so a static spark can damage them.

4.cue: new technical job, ESD be an issue
4.tip: ESD rule: open case + bare chip in hand = wear a wrist strap. RAM is a bare chip.
4.why: Static from your body can damage memory chips you handle directly. Laser printer parts are a high voltage danger to you, not an ESD danger to the PC.

5.cue: preventive maintenance, ESD be an issue
5.tip: Motherboard = the biggest bare circuit board. Biggest board, biggest ESD risk.
5.why: A motherboard is full of exposed chips and traces. Touching it without grounding yourself can send a static spark into those parts and damage them.

7.tip: M.2 SSD is a bare stick of chips plugged into the motherboard. Bare chips = ESD risk.
7.why: An M.2 SSD has no protective case, so its memory chips are exposed while you install it on the motherboard. A static spark could damage it or the board.

8.tip: CPU pins are tiny and sensitive: ground yourself before you touch a processor.
8.why: Installing a processor means handling a bare chip and the open motherboard socket. Static from your hands could damage the CPU's delicate circuits.

72.cue: reboots several times before it eventually starts
72.tip: Random reboots? Think PP: Power supply and Processor.
72.why: A failing power supply can drop voltage and cause restarts, and an overheating or faulty CPU can make the PC reset. BIOS, ROM and NICs don't usually cause reboot loops.

73.cue: working on a spreadsheet, the computer reboots
73.tip: Sudden reboot during work = power or heat. Power supply and CPU.
73.why: If the power supply can't deliver steady power, or the CPU overheats, the computer shuts down and restarts on its own to protect itself.

104.tip: Failed to print = the path is broken: loose cable or the share is gone.
104.why: The job can't reach the printer if the cable is loose or disconnected, or if the network printer has stopped being shared. Either one breaks the path to the printer.

106.tip: Wrong colors? Check the ink: wrong cartridge or dirty print heads.
106.why: Colors come from the ink cartridges and the print heads. A wrong cartridge or clogged, uncalibrated heads mix the colors badly. Cables and ports don't change colors.

107.tip: Faded = not enough toner sticks: low toner or the wrong paper.
107.why: When toner runs low there isn't enough to make dark prints. Paper the printer doesn't support may not hold the toner well, so the print looks pale.

121.tip: Order: Winload finds partition, loads NTOSKRNL and HAL, reads registry and drivers, then the KERNEL takes over.
121.why: After Winload reads the registry and loads device drivers, its job is done, so it hands control to the Windows kernel (NTOSKRNL.EXE).

123.cue: print from laptops and tablets, wireless
123.tip: Printing wirelessly: Wi-Fi (802.11) or Bluetooth. NFC is just a tap, ZigBee is for smart home.
123.why: Laptops and tablets almost all have Wi-Fi (802.11) and Bluetooth, and printers support both for wireless printing. Cellular, ZigBee and NFC aren't used for normal printing.

124.tip: Motherboard must FIT 3 things: the case (size), the power supply (connectors) and the CPU (socket).
124.why: A new board has to fit in the case, get the right connectors from the existing power supply, and have a socket and chipset that work with your CPU. The brand doesn't matter.

125.cue: features of protocols within the TCP/IP stack
125.tip: TCP = Trusty (resends lost data). UDP = Ultra fast, Don't care about Packets lost.
125.why: TCP waits for acknowledgments and resends data that isn't confirmed. UDP skips that checking so it's faster, which suits streaming where a little loss is fine.

keys: does not print a test page
127.tip: Driver = translator. Bad translator prints gibberish or nothing at all.
127.why: The driver turns your document into commands the printer understands. With the wrong driver the printer gets garbled commands, so it prints strange characters or fails the test page.

128.cue: change the wireless router IP address
128.tip: Default settings are public knowledge. Change the default IP so attackers can't guess it.
128.why: Every router of a model ships with the same default IP address, which anyone can look up. Changing it makes it harder for someone to find and log in to the router.

130.cue: laptop and GPS is not functioning
130.tip: GPS broken? First check that the location service is turned ON.
130.why: GPS depends on the location service being enabled. If the service is off or not running, apps can't get a location, so you check its status first.

131.cue: limit the amount of data that the CPU can receive
131.tip: Cache = the CPU's own pocket. A small pocket holds less data at once.
131.why: Cache is very fast memory right on the CPU. Its size limits how much data the CPU can keep close at hand and work on at one time.

132.cue: optical drive greatest amount of storage
132.tip: BD-RE = Blu-ray Rewritable: biggest discs, and it can read and write CDs and DVDs too.
132.why: Blu-ray discs hold the most data, and a BD-RE drive can rewrite them. It also reads and writes older CDs and DVDs. BD-ROM can only read.

133.cue: WINLOGON.EXE displays the Windows Welcome screen (Win 10)
133.tip: Welcome screen = finish line. Nothing comes after it in the boot process.
133.why: Showing the Welcome (logon) screen is the last step of booting. Windows is fully loaded and just waits for you to sign in.

143.tip: NORTHbridge = the fast stuff up top: RAM and video. SOUTHbridge = slow stuff: drives, sound, I/O ports.
143.why: The Northbridge handles the high speed links between the CPU, RAM and the video card. Slower devices like hard drives, sound and I/O ports go through the Southbridge.

144.cue: WINLOGON.EXE displays the Windows Welcome screen (Win 8)
144.tip: Welcome screen = finish line, in every Windows version.
144.why: When WINLOGON.EXE shows the Welcome screen, Windows has finished loading. Booting is complete and the PC waits for a user to log in.

145.cue: WINLOGON.EXE displays the Windows Welcome screen (Win 7)
145.tip: Welcome screen = the last stop. The card reader detail is just noise.
145.why: Displaying the Welcome screen is the final boot step. Extra hardware like a media card reader doesn't change the boot order.

146.cue: restore point, reverse the software installation
146.tip: Restore point -> System Restore. It rolls back the system, not your files.
146.why: System Restore returns Windows settings, programs and drivers to an earlier restore point, but leaves your personal files alone. That undoes the failed install.

147.tip: Before upgrading ask 2 things: Will my APPS run? Will my HARDWARE meet the minimum?
147.why: Old PCs may not have enough RAM or a fast enough CPU for Windows 10, and old or custom programs may not run on it. Both must be checked before upgrading.

148.cue: wireless router settings should be disabled
148.tip: Turn OFF the 3 'easy' features: UPnP, WPS and SSID broadcast. Easy for you is easy for hackers.
148.why: UPnP lets devices open ports without asking, WPS PINs can be cracked, and broadcasting the SSID advertises your network. MAC filtering and parental controls add security.

149.tip: DNS spoofing = the phone book lies: strange DNS server, and the right name takes you to the wrong site.
149.why: DNS turns names into IP addresses. If an attacker fakes DNS, nslookup shows a DNS server you don't recognize and typing cisco.com sends you to a different site.

151.tip: Cloud = rent, don't buy. Less gear and training to pay for, no upgrade or license bills.
151.why: With IaaS and ITaaS the provider owns the equipment and handles upgrades and licenses. You spend less on local hardware, training and software costs.

152.tip: Stop cell data: flip Airplane mode, or switch off Mobile data in Settings.
152.why: Airplane mode turns off all radios, including cellular. The mobile data switch in Settings turns off just cellular data. A hotspot or VPN still uses data.

153.cue: bootable USB hard drive, loads Windows
153.tip: Want to boot from it? Put it FIRST in the boot order. USB hard disk, not USB key.
153.why: The BIOS tries devices in boot order and uses the first one that can boot. Moving the USB Hard Disk option to the top makes it boot Linux whenever the drive is plugged in.

154.tip: Beep codes are a hardware Morse code from POST. Each count points to a different part.
154.why: During POST the BIOS beeps in patterns to report hardware problems it finds, like bad RAM or video. The codes differ between BIOS makers, so you look them up.

155.cue: Microsoft 365, virtual servers leased from a local data center
155.tip: Leased servers in a local data center used only by the college = private cloud.
155.why: The college's own servers, storage and directory run on virtual servers leased just for it, with access control managed locally. Resources used by one organization form a private cloud.

156.cue: displays the Windows installation program screen again
156.tip: Start simple: is the install disc still in the drive?
156.why: If the install disc is still in the drive and boots first, the PC loads the setup program again. Checking the most obvious, easy cause first is good troubleshooting.

157.cue: connect from smart phones, tablets, and laptops
157.tip: Phones and tablets have no Ethernet port. Wireless needs an Access Point.
157.why: An access point lets wireless devices join the wired company network. Phones and tablets connect only by Wi-Fi, so a switch or hub wouldn't help them.

158.tip: Active = it moves (fans use power). Passive = just sits there (heat sink, thermal paste).
158.why: Active cooling uses powered parts, like fans, to move heat away. A heat sink and thermal paste are passive because they cool without using power.

159.tip: Too little RAM = Windows borrows the slow hard drive (paging). Slow drive, slow PC.
159.why: When RAM is full, Windows moves data to a page file on the hard drive. The drive is much slower than RAM, so swapping often makes the computer slow.

160.tip: Shared printers don't appear by magic: each user uses Add a printer and picks it.
160.why: Other users must connect to the shared printer. Using Add a printer and choosing the shared HP printer installs it and its driver from the host PC automatically.

161.cue: separate power connection to directly power the CPU
161.tip: ATX12V = ATX plus an extra 12V plug just for the CPU.
161.why: ATX12V is the most common power supply type. It adds a separate 12 volt connector on the motherboard that feeds the CPU directly. EPS12V is mainly for servers.

162.cue: dialog box pops up requesting a file name
162.tip: Asked for a file name when printing? You're 'printing' to a file, a virtual printer like Print to PDF.
162.why: A virtual printer, such as Microsoft Print to PDF, saves the print job as a file instead of sending it to paper. It's set as default, so nothing reaches the HP printer.

163.cue: single CPU to perform as though two CPUs
163.tip: Hyper-Threading = one core, two threads. It looks like two CPUs.
163.why: Intel's Hyper-Threading lets one core run two streams of instructions at once, so Windows sees two logical CPUs. HyperTransport is an AMD bus, not this.

164.cue: multiple tenants to share the same storage
164.tip: Pool = shared. Many customers swim in the same pool of resources.
164.why: Resource pooling means the provider puts its storage, processing and bandwidth into one pool and shares it among many customers (tenants) as they need it.

165.cue: external ports to connect an external storage
165.tip: The 'e' in eSATA means external. Plain SATA is internal. DVI and HDMI are for video.
165.why: Thunderbolt, USB and eSATA are external ports that carry data to storage drives. SATA is an internal port, and DVI and HDMI only carry video and audio.

166.tip: Power hungry or internal: graphics card, SATA drive, fans. USB stuff gets power from the port.
166.why: Big graphics cards, internal SATA drives and fans need their own power cables. USB flash drives, keyboards and wireless adapters get power through their port or slot.

167.cue: thin clients be a good choice
167.tip: Thin client = thin on its own power, so it needs a FAT network and strong servers.
167.why: Thin clients do little work themselves and rely on servers over the network. They fit low power devices and places with fast LANs and powerful servers, not slow rural links.

168.tip: Type 1 runs on bare metal servers: vSphere, Oracle VM Server. Type 2 runs on a desktop OS: VirtualBox, Workstation.
168.why: The exhibit shows a hypervisor running directly on the hardware (Type 1). VMware vSphere and Oracle VM Server are Type 1. VirtualBox, Virtual PC and Workstation run on top of an OS.

169.cue: can print to the local network printer, but cannot access the cloud
169.tip: Local works, internet fails? Check the gateway. Here it's 192.168.100.1, outside the 192.168.0.x network.
169.why: The PC has 192.168.0.20 /24 but its default gateway is 192.168.100.1, which isn't on its network. Local printing works, but traffic to the internet can't leave. DHCP handed out that gateway.

170.cue: smartwatch shows that it is in discoverable mode
170.tip: Smartwatch pairs over Bluetooth. Watch discoverable but no link? The phone's Bluetooth is off.
170.why: Smartwatches pair with phones over Bluetooth. The watch is ready to be found, so if the phone's Bluetooth is turned off the app can't see or connect to it.

171.cue: DDR SDRAM fastest clock rate, least power
171.tip: Higher DDR number = faster and lower voltage. DDR4 beats DDR3 and DDR2. GDDR5 is for video cards.
171.why: Each new DDR generation runs faster and uses less voltage. DDR4 is the newest here, so it's fastest and most efficient. GDDR5 is graphics memory, not system RAM.

172.tip: The picture is a UEFI/BIOS setup screen. There you set BIOS passwords, not Wi-Fi or screen settings.
172.why: The exhibit shows the UEFI BIOS setup utility. In its security section you can set passwords that control who can enter the BIOS. Screen and Wi-Fi settings are in Windows.

173.cue: short or a termination error in the wiring
173.tip: Cable problem? Cable tester. Shorts, opens, bad wiring: it checks every wire.
173.why: A cable tester checks each wire in a network cable for shorts, breaks and wrong pin order. A tone generator just finds which cable is which.

174.why: Port 110 is the well known port for POP3, the protocol a client uses to download email from a mail server.

175.tip: taskKILL kills tasks. tasklist only lists them.
175.why: taskkill stops running processes, using either their process ID (PID) or their program name. tasklist is the command that just shows what is running.

176.cue: partition scheme that supports storing a backup
176.tip: GPT keeps a Guaranteed Partition Table backup. MBR has only one copy.
176.why: GPT stores a main partition table at the start of the disk and a backup copy at the end. If one gets damaged, the other can be used to recover.

177.cue: MBR be partitioned to support additional logical drives
177.tip: MBR has 4 slots. Turn one into an EXTENDED partition, a box that holds logical drives.
177.why: MBR allows only four primary partitions. Making one of them an extended partition lets you create many logical drives inside it.

179.cue: variables contained in the sample.sh script
179.tip: 'read uname' = the script asks you, so it's input. $HOSTNAME and $HOME come from the system.
179.why: The script uses 'read uname' to store what you type, so $uname is an input variable made in the script. $HOSTNAME isn't set in the script, Linux sets it as an environment variable.

181.cue: Windows kernel takes over (Win 7, cellular SIM)
181.tip: Kernel takes over -> NTOSKRNL starts WINLOGON -> Welcome screen. K then L: Kernel, then Login.
181.why: Once the kernel (NTOSKRNL.EXE) is in control, it starts WINLOGON.EXE, which then shows the Welcome screen so you can sign in.

182.cue: secure method of erasing the data
182.tip: Flash memory isn't magnetic, so degaussing does nothing. Use secure erase software.
182.why: Secure erase tools overwrite every memory cell so data can't be recovered. A quick format only removes the file list, and magnets don't affect flash drives.

183.cue: contents of the ite_user home directory
keys: two data files and three directories
183.tip: In ls -l, a leading '-' is a file and 'd' is a directory. Count: 2 dashes, 3 d's.
183.why: The listing shows January and February starting with '-' (files) and Newfiles, Test1 and Test2 starting with 'd' (directories). The files have sizes, so they do hold data.

185.tip: PHI leaves the clinic = breach. Screenshots of records or copies of patient data sent away both count.
185.why: Protected health information can't be shared or copied outside the clinic without permission. Screenshots of real records and backups moved to an IT office both expose patient data.

186.tip: del = DELete files. rd removes directories, move relocates files.
186.why: The del command deletes one or more files in a Windows directory. Removing an empty directory is rd, and relocating a file is move.

187.tip: Frozen app? Do what you'd do with any frozen device: reset it.
187.why: A reset (restart) clears memory and stops stuck processes, so an app that isn't responding usually works again. Turning off Bluetooth or Wi-Fi won't fix a hung app.

188.cue: recover an older version of a document
188.tip: File History = history of your FILES. System Restore = system settings, not documents.
188.why: File History saves copies of your files over time, so you can open an earlier version from the same day. System Restore doesn't touch personal files.

189.cue: change the file system to NTFS without losing the data
189.tip: convert X: /fs:ntfs turns FAT32 into NTFS and keeps your files.
189.why: The convert command changes a FAT32 drive to NTFS in place, keeping the files on it. Reformatting or making a new partition would erase the data.

190.cue: local backup of iPhone data on a Windows laptop
190.tip: iPhone + Windows = iTunes. Finder and Time Machine are Mac tools.
190.why: On a Windows PC, Apple's iTunes is used to back up and sync an iPhone. Finder and Time Machine only exist on Macs, and Google sync is for Android.

191.tip: Storage Spaces = pool your drives into one big space, like software RAID.
191.why: Storage Spaces lets you group several drives into a storage pool and set them up as arrays that can protect data, similar to RAID, all from inside Windows.

192.cue: not restored when using Windows Restore
192.tip: Restore fixes the SYSTEM, never your stuff. Your documents stay as they are.
192.why: A restore point covers system files, drivers, the registry and program settings. Personal data files are left alone, so they aren't rolled back or lost.

193.tip: Boot order starts: POST, then BIOS reads CMOS settings, then it finds a boot drive.
193.why: After the power-on self-test checks hardware, the BIOS reads its saved settings from CMOS memory, such as the boot order, before it looks for a drive to boot from.

194.tip: More cores = more work at once. Great for games and video editing.
194.why: A multicore CPU runs several tasks in parallel, so it finishes work faster than a single core. Heavy apps like games and video editors take advantage of that.

195.tip: MAC = burned into the NIC, never changes. To reach the internet you need a public IP.
195.why: A MAC address is built into the network card, so it stays the same on every network. Internet routers only forward public addresses, so a public IPv4 or IPv6 address is required.

196.cue: laptop screen flickers and appears dull
196.tip: External monitor fine, laptop screen dim? The light is the problem: backlight or inverter.
196.why: The external monitor looks normal, so the GPU works. A dim, flickering laptop screen points to its lighting: the backlight or the inverter that powers it.

197.tip: New power supply: does it FIT (size) and is it STRONG enough (wattage)?
197.why: The replacement has to fit in the case and give enough watts to run every part in the computer. UPS and eSATA support aren't power supply features.

198.tip: Unbuffered = no middleman. Data goes straight to the CPU, so it's faster. Buffered is for big servers.
198.why: Buffered RAM has an extra chip between the memory and the controller, which adds a small delay. Unbuffered RAM is read directly, so it's faster for home and gaming PCs.

199.cue: UTM appliance, such as a Cisco ASA 5506-X
199.tip: UTM = Unified Threat Management: security tools in one box, like firewall plus IPS/IDS.
199.why: A UTM appliance combines several security devices, including a stateful firewall and an intrusion prevention or detection system. It isn't a modem, storage drive or big switch.

200.cue: replaces the memory, does not resolve the performance
200.tip: Fix didn't work? Write it down and put the original part back before trying the next idea.
200.why: Since the new memory didn't help, you put the original memory back so you don't add new variables, and you document that this attempt failed before testing the next cause.

201.cue: VirtualBox to run automatically when Windows 10 starts
201.tip: Want it to start with Windows? Drop its shortcut in the Startup folder.
201.why: Windows runs every shortcut in the Startup folder when you sign in. Task Manager's Startup tab can only enable or disable programs already listed, not add new ones.

202.cue: web-based application was no longer functioning
202.tip: Before you leave: VERIFY that everything works, not just the thing you fixed.
202.why: After a fix you must test the whole system. The new antivirus likely broke the web app, and checking full system functionality would have caught it before leaving.

203.tip: Hotend: heat depends on the filament, and nozzles wear out like ink.
203.why: Each filament type melts at its own temperature, so the nozzle heats to match. Nozzles wear and clog over time, so they're consumables you replace in normal maintenance.

204.cue: What can be determined from the output
204.tip: January is -rw-rw-r--: r for owner, r for group, r for others. Everyone can read.
204.why: The permissions for January are rw- for owner, rw- for group and r-- for others. Each group has an r, so all three can read the file. There are 2 files and 3 directories.

205.cue: very fast boot and high capacity storage
205.tip: SSHD = SSD + HDD in one drive: SSD speed for booting, HDD space for storage.
205.why: A solid state hybrid drive has a small flash section for fast access, like booting, and a large spinning disk for lots of storage. It mixes both benefits.

206.cue: require the width of two slots
206.tip: Big fans and heat sinks = graphics card. That's why it takes two slots.
206.why: Powerful graphics cards make a lot of heat, so they carry large heat sinks and fans. That cooling makes them two slots wide even though they plug into one PCIe x16 slot.

207.tip: Discoverable = saying 'Hi, I'm Speaker X, and here's what I can do.'
207.why: In discoverable mode a Bluetooth device broadcasts its name and what it supports, so the laptop can list it and start pairing. A PIN may come later, not in the broadcast.

208.cue: BIOS locates and reads the configuration settings
keys: first drive that contains a valid boot sector
208.tip: POST, read CMOS, then boot from the FIRST drive with a valid boot sector.
208.why: Once the BIOS has read its CMOS settings, it follows the boot order and starts from the first drive that has a valid boot sector.

209.cue: Windows kernel takes over (Win 7, SIM slot)
209.tip: Kernel in charge -> it starts WINLOGON. Kernel, then Login.
209.why: After the Windows kernel takes control, NTOSKRNL.EXE starts WINLOGON.EXE, the program that handles the logon and shows the Welcome screen.

210.tip: bootrec = BOOT RECovery. It fixes the MBR and boot records.
210.why: bootrec is a recovery tool that repairs boot problems, such as a damaged master boot record (bootrec /fixmbr). diskpart manages drives and format prepares them.

211.cue: Windows kernel takes over (Win 7, 4 GB RAM)
211.tip: Kernel takes over -> starts WINLOGON -> Welcome screen. The 4 GB RAM detail doesn't matter.
211.why: Right after the kernel takes control, NTOSKRNL.EXE starts WINLOGON.EXE. The Welcome screen comes one step later, after WINLOGON runs.

212.tip: gpRESULT shows the RESULT of group policy. gpUPDATE refreshes it.
212.why: gpresult displays which group policy settings are applied to the user and computer, so you can check settings you think are wrong. gpupdate applies new policies.

213.cue: WinLoad loads two files: NTOSKRNL.EXE and HAL.DLL
213.tip: Winload order: find partition, load kernel and HAL, read REGISTRY and drivers, hand to kernel.
213.why: After loading NTOSKRNL.EXE and HAL.DLL, Winload reads the registry, picks a hardware profile and loads the drivers. Only then does the kernel take over.

214.cue: control of the boot process is given to Windows Boot Manager
214.tip: Boot Manager (BOOTMGR) points the way, then Winload follows that path to the boot partition.
214.why: Once Windows Boot Manager is running, Winload uses the path that BOOTMGR gives it to find the Windows boot partition, and then it loads the kernel files.

215.tip: App won't load? Restart the device first. Display settings don't stop apps.
215.why: A reset restarts the device, clears memory and ends stuck processes. That often lets an app load again. Display or refresh settings don't affect whether apps load.

216.cue: file system that supports a partition size up to 2 TB
216.tip: FAT32 is the only FILE SYSTEM in the list. Formatting, dynamic and basic disk are not file systems.
216.why: FAT32 is a file system, and the course says its partitions can be up to 2 TB. Formatting is a process, and basic and dynamic disks are disk types, not file systems.

217.cue: Why would a technician need to use the copy command
217.tip: copy = make a duplicate in a new place. move = relocate it.
217.why: The copy command copies files from one location to another, leaving the originals in place. Moving or relocating files is done with move.

297.cue: Touch ID or Face ID additional verification
297.tip: iPhone biometrics always have a backup: the passcode.
297.why: iOS requires you to set a passcode before using Touch ID or Face ID. It's the backup when your face or finger can't be read, and it's needed after a restart.

298.cue: prevented by creating a UEFI password
298.tip: UEFI password locks the UEFI settings, like boot order. It doesn't stop malware or phishing.
298.why: A UEFI password stops people from changing firmware settings. Without it someone could change the boot order and boot another OS to get around Windows security.

307.cue: Why would a gamer need to use the copy command
307.tip: copy = duplicate. The original stays where it is.
307.why: The copy command duplicates files to another location. Preparing a drive is format's job, and managing disks and partitions is diskpart's job.

327.tip: gpUPDATE = UPDATE group policy now. gpresult = show the result.
327.why: gpupdate makes the PC refresh and apply the latest group policy settings right away, instead of waiting for the automatic refresh.

330.tip: GPT goes with UEFI and keeps a backup table. MBR goes with BIOS and has a 2 TB limit.
330.why: GPT is the partition style used with UEFI firmware, and it stores a backup copy of the partition table. The 2 TB limit and single table belong to MBR.

331.cue: reset option, retain the user's personal files
331.tip: Reset + Keep my files = Windows reinstalled, your files kept, your apps gone.
331.why: Reset this PC with Keep my files reinstalls Windows and keeps your personal files. Installed apps and settings are removed, so only user files come back.

keys: not a member of the administrator group
332.tip: Run as Administrator only works if you ARE an administrator.
332.why: Running something with elevated permission needs administrator rights. If the user isn't in the Administrators group, Windows won't grant them, so the action fails.

335.tip: Kernel takes over -> NTOSKRNL starts WINLOGON -> then the Welcome screen.
335.why: After the kernel is in control, NTOSKRNL.EXE starts WINLOGON.EXE. Displaying the Welcome screen is the step after that, so it's not next yet.

338.tip: A library is a playlist for folders: it shows many folders in one place.
338.why: A Windows library gathers several folders from different locations into one view, without moving the files. It doesn't change file name length or encryption.

340.tip: Motherboard swap = lots of bare circuits. Ground yourself first.
340.why: Replacing a motherboard means handling a big board full of exposed chips. A static discharge from your body can damage them, so you use an antistatic wrist strap.

344.cue: Windows 10 boot sequence after the boot manager
344.tip: W-N-R-K-W: Winload, NTOSKRNL and HAL, Registry and drivers, Kernel takes over, Winlogon.
344.why: Boot manager starts Winload, which loads the kernel and HAL, then reads the registry and drivers. The kernel then takes over and finally starts Winlogon for the sign-in.
